VeyyonONE: where your data lives today, and where it should live

A plain-language look at the database behind the app, what we recommend changing, and what each choice gains and costs you.

In short

  • Today's setup is fine for one user. It has two weak points once several people enter money at the same time.
  • We recommend fixing those two points now, in the current system.
  • We recommend moving to a PostgreSQL database with a server layer as the app grows towards ten users. That is a planned project, not an emergency.

Today

The app on each phone and laptop talks straight to a Google database called Firestore. There is no server of your own in between. All the calculations happen on each person's device.

Phones and laptopsThe app does all the work here: totals, GST, TDS, balances, invoice numbers
direct connection, no server in between
Database access rulesThe only gate deciding who may read or change what
reads and writes
Firestore database (Google)About 30 separate lists of records. Records point to each other by name, not by a fixed ID. Attachments are stored inside the database.
Sign-inGoogle Firebase
Nightly backupA script copies data to Google Drive
Phone alertsA small program reads the data every few minutes

What is good about it

  • Very low running cost, and nothing to maintain.
  • Google keeps the data safe and available.
  • The app keeps working with a poor or no connection.
  • Everyone sees changes within about a second.
  • It is already built and working.

What is weak about it

  • A payment can be lost. If two people add a payment to the same project at the same moment, or one of them was offline, one entry can silently disappear.
  • Two invoices can get the same number. Each device picks the next number by itself.
  • One gate only. If an access rule is wrong, nothing else stops a signed-in person reading or changing data.
  • No "see only your own" option. A role either sees a whole list or none of it. Hiding single fields, such as cost, is not possible.
  • Links can break. Rename a client or project and older records may no longer match.
  • It slows with volume. Every device downloads every record each time the app opens.

Proposed

The app stops talking to the database directly. A server layer sits in the middle, checks every request, and does the money calculations in one place. The data moves into PostgreSQL, a database built for linked business records.

Phones and laptopsThe app shows screens and collects input only
every request is checked
Server layerConfirms who you are and what your role allows. Calculates totals, GST and TDS. Issues invoice and PO numbers one at a time.
only the server can reach the database
PostgreSQL databaseAbout 45 linked tables. Every invoice is tied to its project and client by a fixed ID. Each payment is its own row. A second set of access rules lives here too.
Sign-inPart of the same platform
File storageAttachments kept outside the database
Automatic backupsRestore to any point in recent days
Phone alertsAsks the database only for what is due

What you gain

  • Payments cannot overwrite each other.
  • Invoice and PO numbers are never duplicated or skipped by accident.
  • Two layers of protection in place of one.
  • Access down to the record and the field: a BD person sees only their leads; a manager sees a project without its cost.
  • Renaming a client never breaks older records.
  • Reports across leads, projects, invoices and payments come from one query, and every device shows the same figure.
  • A record of who changed what on money entries.
  • Stays fast as records grow.

What it costs you

  • A real project. The way the app reads and saves data has to be rebuilt. The screens can largely stay.
  • A monthly hosting fee for the database and server.
  • Less offline working. Viewing can still work offline; entering money would need a connection.
  • A one-time data move, including tidying client names that are spelled differently in different places.
  • Someone technical on call. There is now a server to look after.

How the data is reorganised

Nothing is thrown away. The same information is stored in a stricter shape.

AreaTodayProposed
ClientsTyped as text on each lead, quote, project and invoiceOne client list that everything else points to
Quotes, invoices, POsLine items kept inside each documentEach line item is its own row, so it can be totalled and reported
Money in and outA list kept inside each project, PO or billOne row per receipt or payment, linked to its invoice and bank entry
Roles and accessA settings record read by the appTables the database itself enforces
Payroll, attendance, timesheetsSeparate listsLinked to each employee and project
AttachmentsSplit into pieces inside the databaseKept in file storage, with a pointer in the database

How we would get there

  1. Now  Finish the security review. Fix the lost-payment and duplicate-number gaps in the current system. Until then, have one person enter payments and raise invoices, and only when online.
  2. Design  Agree the table design and the access rules for each role, on paper, before anything is built.
  3. Build  Build the server layer and the new database. Copy your existing data across and check the totals match.
  4. Trial  Run both side by side for a short period, with the current system as the fallback.
  5. Switch  Move everyone over and keep the old data as a read-only archive.

What we need you to decide

  1. Timing. Move before the team grows, or stay on the current system for the first months and move later?
  2. Offline entry. Is it acceptable that payments and invoices can only be entered with a connection?
  3. Who sees what. For each role, which records and which figures should be hidden? We will bring a simple grid to fill in.
  4. Client names. Are you willing to review a list of duplicate or differently spelled client names once, during the move?

Based on a review of the app's code at version 36.45. The database access rules and the backup script have been requested and are not yet reviewed, so the security points above describe the design, not a confirmed fault.
